title: Ang 10–12: So Purakh
hookLine: the Rehras hymns of Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan
tomorrow: why do the night prayers come before the first raga?

lines: HIS TURN IN THE FAMILY'S READING.
cards: Dusk at a truck stop off the interstate. Engines idling, the sky going orange over the pumps. A driver props his phone against the steering wheel.
It's his turn in the family's reading, and he's doing it from a few states away. He scrolls past So Dar and slows down. The heading has changed: Mahala 4.
The hymn opens, so purakh niranjan, and he reads to the end of the verse. The name there is Nanak. But the heading says four.

teach.b: Mahala 4 means the fourth Guru: Guru Ram Das. Here's the thing to tell someone tonight.
The Gurus who came after Guru Nanak signed their hymns with his name, Nanak. So the name in the verse stays the same, and the heading's number tells you whose voice it is.
Sikhs say the same light passed from Guru to Guru, and the shared name fits that. Now the hymn itself.
So purakh niranjan: that Being, spotless, without a stain. In paraphrase, the hymn goes on: all meditate on You, true Creator; every being is Yours, and You give to every being.
These are the So Purakh hymns, part of the Rehras, the evening prayer. Then, on ang twelve, the heading changes again: Mahala 5, Guru Arjan.
And a line that lands at dusk, in the original: gobind milan kee eh teree bareeaa.
This is your turn to meet the Lord of the universe.
So in a few evening pages, three Gurus speak, one name runs through them, and the last word is about now. The driver at the pump keeps reading.

how: Sikhs say the Rehras at dusk, at home or in the gurdwara; in the Guru Granth Sahib its hymns begin with So Dar on ang 8 and continue with So Purakh, by Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, on angs 10 to 12.

games.q: reading with your family, you reach a hymn signed Nanak under the heading Mahala 5. your cousin says it must be Guru Nanak's. what do you tell him?
o: he's right: the name in the verse settles it.
it's Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru; the heading's number says so.
it's a later poet who happened to be called Nanak.
games.why: the Gurus after Guru Nanak signed as Nanak. the heading's mahala number tells you whose voice it is: here, the fifth Guru.

practice: If you can, open to ang ten and read the first line, so purakh niranjan, once. Then close your eyes and let the day settle, the way the sky settles at dusk.
When a thought from today comes up, set it down beside you and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Ang 10. Where So Purakh begins: the evening pages, in the voice of the fourth Guru. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: mahala, the word in a hymn's heading followed by a number that names the Guru speaking.

carryVoice: For the road: the evening pages, where many voices sign the one name. Sleep well tonight.
